summary.text: The Permian–Triassic extinction struck around the boundary between the Permian and Triassic periods and is Earth's most severe known extinction event.
It killed 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species, and it is also the greatest known mass extinction of insects.
The scientific consensus blames the Siberian Traps eruptions, whose gases raised global temperatures, acidified the oceans and left them oxygen-starved and sulfurous.

facts.label: Boundary fossil marker
facts.value: First appearance of the conodont Hindeodus parvus

items.prompt: Right at the boundary, some rocks show a sudden surge in the remains of fungi. What has been proposed to explain it?

options.label: A sharp rise in dead plants and animals for fungi to feed on
A cold snap that killed every bacterium competing with fungi
Ash from eruptions that fungi used directly as food
Rising sea levels that carried fungi far inland

items.explain: The boundary has been linked to a jump in marine and land fungi, caused by the sharp increase in dead plants and animals they fed on.

items.prompt: A geologist has rock layers that cannot be dated radiometrically. What could still help her find the Permian–Triassic boundary?

options.label: A thin clay layer rich in iridium
An abrupt drop in carbon-13 relative to carbon-12
The first dinosaur footprints in the layers
A thick band of deposits left by glaciers

items.explain: A large, abrupt global drop in δ¹³C, the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12, coincides with the extinction and is used to identify the boundary in rocks unsuitable for radiometric dating.

items.prompt: Giant volcanic eruptions on land went on for a long time. How could they kill life throughout the oceans?

options.label: Lava flowed into the sea and boiled it worldwide
Volcanic ash buried the sea floor everywhere at once
Their gases heated the planet, acidified the seas and stripped oxygen
The eruptions drained the oceans into cracks in the crust

items.explain: The Siberian Traps released sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide, leading to higher global temperatures, acidified oceans and oxygen-starved, sulfurous seas.

items.prompt: Is it settled whether life on land and life in the sea died off at the same time?

options.label: Yes, all evidence shows they happened together
No, studies disagree, and some find land losses came first
Yes, all evidence shows the sea died off first
No, because no land fossils from the time survive

items.explain: Whether land and sea extinctions were synchronous is disputed: some sequences show them starting together, while other scientists think the land extinction began earlier.

items.prompt: Why is it hard to tell which losses belong to the Permian–Triassic event itself?

options.label: Rocks this old can never be dated more finely than millions of years
Almost no rock layers from the boundary have been found anywhere
An earlier late-Permian extinction came shortly before it
The boundary is defined differently on every continent

items.explain: The Capitanian extinction closely preceded the event, and many extinctions once dated to the Permian–Triassic boundary have been re-dated to it.

items.prompt: Roughly what share of marine species died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction?

options.label: About 21%
About 45%
About 63%
About 81%

items.explain: It is Earth's most severe known extinction event, with 81% of marine species lost.
